newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine business protests tax closures bill.
newsitem.headline: Argentine business protests tax closures bill.

text.p: Argentine businesses and unions on Thursday protested a bill now in Congress that would empower the tax office to close firms for three days if they are caught making a sale without a receipt.
The bill, approved by the Chamber of Deputies late Wednesday and passed on to the Senate, would also impose fines on shoppers who fail to produce receipts for purchases if asked by tax authorities.

About 200 members of small and medium-sized business lobby groups, supported by members of the CTA union which opposes the Peronist government, staged a rally outside the DGI tax office's headquarters in Buenos Aires' landmark Plaza de Mayo.

Ruben Manusovich, head of the Fedecamaras shopkeepers' group, called a protest blackout for January 16 and urged members to manifest their discontest at the polling booths when Peronist President Carlos Menem's second term ends in 1999.

Jorge Di Fiori, head of the Argentine Chamber of Commerce, told reporters separately the bill "violates the constitution" by giving the tax office the powers of a court of law. "And it won't increase tax revenues," he said.
The law is designed to give tax chief Carlos Silvani new powers to crack down on tax evasion in a country where it runs at nearly $20 billion a year -- or half the national budget.
Tax inspectors would be able to shut a business for three days the first time they are caught failing to give a receipt, 10-20 days the second time, and up to a month the third time.
Shoppers would be fined 10-20 percent of the cost of the merchandise they bought the first time, rising to 20-30 percent the second time, and 30-40 percent the third time.
Penalties are for transactions valued at more than $10. The law also provides for $500 to $20,000 fines for businesses that fail to keep all records on its transactions.
Di Fiori recognized that Congress had watered down the penalties of the original bill, but said, "That just means a little moderation in applying an unconstitutional sanction."
